meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It ain't what you don't know that gets you into trouble. It's what you know for sure that just ain't so'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Reagan. Quote Investigator traces this anonymous line to Josh Billings (1874); it's serially misattributed to Twain, Rogers, and Hubbard.

answer.label: Not Ronald Reagan — an anonymous saying rooted in Josh Billings
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording is not Ronald Reagan’s, and its true author is anonymous. Per Quote Investigator, the earliest documented root is humorist Josh Billings, who wrote in 1874, “I honestly believe it is better to know nothing than to know what ain’t so.” The polished modern sentence evolved anonymously and has been serially pinned on Mark Twain, Will Rogers, and Kin Hubbard. Reagan did voice a related idea in his 1964 “A Time for Choosing” speech — “the trouble with our liberal friends… is just that they know so much that isn’t so” — but that is a different line, and he claimed no authorship of this saying.

source.excerpt: It ain’t what you don’t know that gets you into trouble. It’s what you know for sure that just ain’t so.
trail: The definitive study is Quote Investigator, which finds the creator “remains anonymous” and traces the earliest matching form to Josh Billings’s 1874 collection.
QI documents the wandering credits: Mark Twain (1899), Artemus Ward (1911), Josh Billings (1913), Kin Hubbard (1958), and Will Rogers (1978) — none with substantive support, per Quote Investigator.

Reagan’s genuine, and different, line appears in the Reagan Library transcript of “A Time for Choosing” (27 Oct 1964): “The trouble with our liberal friends is not that they’re ignorant; it’s just that they know so much that isn’t so.”
source.excerptNote: The polished modern form above is anonymous. The nearest genuine ancestor is Josh Billings’s 1874 line: “I honestly believe it is better to know nothing than to know what ain’t so.”

source.rightsNote: The exact modern wording has no identifiable author or first-publication, so no copyright status can be asserted for it. Its 1874 Josh Billings ancestor is long in the public domain, whereas Reagan’s separate 1964 “A Time for Choosing” wording is in copyright — but neither is the sentence quoted here.

author.name: Josh Billings (Henry Wheeler Shaw)
author.heading: About Josh Billings (Henry Wheeler Shaw)
author.bio: Henry Wheeler Shaw, writing as Josh Billings, was one of 19th-century America’s most popular humorists, famous for aphorisms in comic phonetic spelling. His 1874 Everybody’s Friend carried the line — “better to know nothing than to know what ain’t so” — that Quote Investigator identifies as the earliest documented root of this saying. He is credited here as its nearest genuine ancestor, though the polished modern wording is anonymous.

misattribution.heading: A quote that proves its own point
misattribution.intro: Fittingly for a line about believing things that just ain’t so, this saying is one of the most misattributed in English. Quote Investigator finds no evidence any of its famous claimants wrote it.

items.why: The single most popular credit online, but scholars at the Center for Mark Twain Studies find no support, and QI records the Twain ascription only from 1899 onward — long after the idea was circulating. Quote Investigator.

Reagan said a related thought in 1964 — “they know so much that isn’t so” — but not this sentence, and he claimed no authorship. Crediting him with this exact wording is a modern mix-up. Reagan Library.

items.who: Will Rogers, Kin Hubbard, Artemus Ward
items.why: All picked up the line at various points (Rogers in a 1978 magazine, Hubbard via Laurence J. Peter in 1977), with no substantive evidence any coined it. Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The nearest genuine author is Josh Billings, whose 1874 “better to know nothing than to know what ain’t so” is the earliest documented form; the crisp modern sentence itself is anonymous, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why this line keeps getting a new author
lead: A pithy, folksy aphorism with no famous name attached is unstable: retellers reach for a recognizable humorist to lend it authority. Over 150 years the same sentence has been handed to Twain, Ward, Billings, Hubbard, Rogers — and, more recently, to Reagan, whose 1964 “they know so much that isn’t so” gave the sentiment a memorable political home.
context.pull: A saying about false certainty that nobody can say for sure who wrote.
